Thank you for submitting your article "Nitric oxide radicals are emitted by wasp eggs to kill mold fungi" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Ian Baldwin as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Your manuscript addresses a very interesting study on how a beewolf preserves the bees that it has collected and protects them from degenerating by the provisioning of NO· by the eggs. All three reviewers provide positive evaluations of your study. Yet, some aspects require further improvement, including an essential additional experiment.

The main issues to be resolved are:

1) The study focuses on NO·, thereby potentially missing other active compounds as highlighted by reviewer 2. To assess the role of NO·, additional evidence to support NO· as being the causal agent is needed, i.e. eliminating NO· with the inhibitor as suggested by reviewer 3. This additional experiment will provide essential information to conclude on the effect of NO· within the total characteristics of the egg.

2) The discussion on the NO· levels in the brood cell, leaking in the soil, survival of larvae and later developmental stages of the wasp, survival of the bees beyond day 3 etc. is not satisfactory. See comments by reviewers 1 and 2. Especially the brief mentioning of mortality of larvae needs more attention and clarification as this is vital for understanding the functioning of NO· as a true resource protectant.

3) The discussion on the NOS gene and its uniqueness in the beewolf. Please clarify what makes the detected NOS gene substantially different from its orthologues and therefore capable of performing a different function (higher NOS production), and better address the option that NO· might arise from different genes.

In addition, the reviewers have made other valuable comments that will be helpful in further improving the manuscript.

Reviewer #1:

This manuscript provides a very interesting study of how beewolf eggs may prevent bee supplies from fungal colonisation by producing high levels of NO· radicals. The study shows that the presence of beewolf eggs prevents mold growth on paralyzed honeybees in the brood cells, that NO· is produced in the eggs, is present around the paralyzed bees and that eggs prevent the growth of a fungus, i.e. Aspergillus flavus. Yet, some important questions remain to fully understand how NO· radicals protect the bees while not harming the beewolf larva or its symbiotic bacteria.

Although the evidence supports the beewolf egg as a source of NO·, the data cannot exclude that NO· is also produced by the paralyzed bee on which the egg has been deposited. The data presented in Figure 2B would support this, as well as the data in Figure 4B. Why was no experiment included in which mold growth on a bee was recorded in the presence of an egg that was presented without a bee substrate to supplement the data in Figure 2B? The data in Figure 4B show that NO· is present on a bee on which an egg has been laid but it cannot be excluded that part of this is produced by the bee.

The manuscript does not present all data and some crucial data are presented as supplementary figures. Why are not all crucial data presented in the main text? For instance (a) the data for the 5 additional fungi are not presented at all (Results, first paragraph), (b) Subsection “Identification of the antifungal volatile”, last paragraph, please show these data, there is no space limitation, (c) Subsection “Identification of the antifungal volatile”, last paragraph: why is the data of the Griese analysis of the headspace samples not presented?, (d) Figures 9 and 10 provide support for the production of NO· in the beewolf egg; the picture (Figure 9) is a combination of two pictures (why?); what is the age of the egg shown in Figure 9 (very important in the context of Figure 10 and Figure 5)? (e) fungus growth inhibition was recorded at 24, 48 and 72 hours (subsection “Fungus inhibition assays”, last paragraph) but no data for 48 or 72 h are presented.

In Figure 6, please provide the exact P value for the comparison between control and D-NAME instead of stating that it is > 0.05.

The picture in Figure 3 presents only one replication. How many replicates were there and how similar were the results? Preferably the pictures of the replicates should be presented in a supplementary figure. The number of replications is low for some experiments, e.g. for timing of NO· emission only 4 replicates were used but for the iodometry experiment a large number of eggs (233) has been used.

Please add a note on the number of replications to the legend of Figure 6 and Figure 10.

The discussion on how the beewolf eggs and the Streptomyces bacteria survive the high NO· levels is not convincing to me. The authors first argue that the NO· concentrations in the brood cell are way too high for fungi to develop resistance (Discussion, twelfth paragraph) but then state that potentially the Streptomyces bacteria are resistant to the NO·, maybe helped by being at the ceiling of the brood cell. However, given the dimensions and the average very high NO· concentration the concentration near the ceiling is likely still very high. Moreover, the arguments given for how the beewolf larvae may survive the high concentrations (Discussion) are not convincing; after all they are the source of the high levels being emitted and even as larva they are killed by these high concentrations.

How do the larvae that emerge from the NO· producing eggs survive in the brood cell? The comment in the twelfth paragraph of the Discussion suggests they do not, which would imply that the NO· concentration drops with time if the larvae are to survive. If that is true (is it?) then how are the bees protected from molding during days 3-11 when the larva develops (Figure 1)? The study provides information on NO· production with time but not on NO· concentration during the 11 days of larval development, which would be needed for this.

The manuscript should provide answers to these questions to be fully convincing on the protective effect of egg-produced high NO· concentrations in terms of preventing their food to be infested by molds while they themselves should survive the intoxicated brood cell.

Reviewer #2:

In this interesting manuscript, Strohm et al. propose a new mechanism of brood defense from fungal pathogens based on the production of antifungal volatile compounds. This is a novel and potentially important idea that offers new insights into how insects might combat pathogens during vulnerable life cycle stages. On the whole, I enjoyed reading this well-written manuscript and the ideas that it contains. However, I was left with some questions that I hope the authors can address:

1) Given the existence of other defense mechanisms in the beewolf system, is there any potential for NO production to interact synergistically or antagonistically with these other defense mechanisms? For example, are there any compounds on the eggs themselves that might provide some antifungal activity? A broader discussion (e.g., in the Introduction) of the various beewolf defense mechanisms and their importance in different phases of the beewolf life cycle might help clarify these issues. This issue also intersects with the discussion of NO resistance by the Streptomyces symbiont, such that there might be trade-offs between defenses active at different life cycle stages.

2) The author's focus on NO is quite directed, and so might cause them to miss other potential volatile compounds that are also involved in the observed bioactivities. Better justifying this approach would be valuable. There also seems to be some disconnect between the first paragraph of the subsection “Identification of the antifungal volatile”, where the authors seem to interpret the odor given off by the beewolf eggs as similar to NO2, and the first paragraph of the subsection “Identification of the antimicrobial volatile”, where samples where nitrate was reduced to detect NO2 did not differ from those that were not reduced, implying that only NO (and not NO2) was produced by the eggs, despite the odor.

3) The authors' calculations of likely NO concentrations in brood cells is very interesting, but I am unsure how likely these values are to relate to the actual values in the wild. In particular, how likely is it that there is "no loss due to reactions or leaking out of the confined space of brood cells”? It seems that soil could conceivably be quite porous and so allow NO to escape the brood cell. A pulse that diffuses quickly would impact the need for and nature of NO resistance mechanisms that the authors discuss extensively. Similarly, what is the likely soil temperature of a typical beewolf brood cell? The assay temperatures strike me as being warmer than many soils in temperate Europe, although I imagine that the insect could select appropriate sites to meet this constraint. Finally, the authors propose oxic mechanisms for NO (bio)chemistry (e.g., conversion of NO to NO2) without specifying if the brood cells are oxic or anoxic. Reduced oxygen in brood cells seems plausible if they are sealed while the egg is developing (and presumably respiring).

4) The authors give several potential mechanisms for NO resistance, but it is unclear how plausible these are given the potentially high concentrations of NO that might be present. A more quantitative discussion of NO resistance would be helpful here, e.g., are the proposed resistance mechanisms likely to be sufficient under the proposed levels of NO accumulation?

5) Discussion, twelfth paragraph: the authors propose that coating the symbiotic Streptomyces in hydrocarbons might protect them from NO toxicity. However, the bees are also coated in hydrocarbons (Introduction, fourth paragraph). Wouldn't the resistance mechanism proposed for the bacteria then also protect fungi growing on the bees? Antioxidants are also proposed to be mixed with these hydrocarbons – how likely are these to exist?

6) Discussion, fifteenth paragraph: the observation that larvae are not resistant to NO produced by the eggs is concerning. Are other life cycle stages similarly sensitive to NO, e.g., eggs exposed before they start producing NO or immediately after? The sensitivity of larvae might imply that NO does not accumulate in the brood cells for very long (see also my comment #3 above).

7) I am not entirely clear how to interpret Figure 9 because I am unclear what baseline level of staining to expect before NOS induction. Comparisons between time points and/or other species where NOS is not thought to be induced would provide useful controls for this experiment.

8) The focus on the detected NOS gene as being responsible for the observed NOS activity makes the argument that this gene behaves differently compared to all other known genes without direct evidence for such divergent behavior. The one inferred splice variant by itself seems to provide weak evidence for higher activity, given that higher NOS activity observed in humans is due to different genes (vs. splice variants of the same gene) and that NOS activity in humans is of a different order of magnitude than implied here for beewolves. The inhibition experiment provides some evidence for NOS being involved, although there is still the assumption that NOS is the only enzyme affected by the inhibitor. Differential gene expression matching NO production, direct assays of the NOS variants, or even signatures of adaptive evolution (e.g., Dn/Ds metrics) would provide more convincing support for the uniqueness of the beewolf NOS, especially when combined with explicit comparisons to related species that due not produce similarly high levels of NO as controls.

Reviewer #3:

This is a very nice paper that touches on different fascinating aspects of insect's biology, from an ecological to a molecular point of view, and should interest a broad audience.

This study shows that eggs of the parasitic wasp Philanthus triangulum emit high amounts of nitric oxide as antifungal compounds to protect themselves and preserve the food source of their progeny. The enzyme responsible for NO production is identified (NOS) and a differential splicing event between egg and adult forms may explain the high levels observed in eggs. These are novel and quite interesting findings that complement other defense strategies that have been previously reported in insects. The story is well written and nicely presented. Data are convincing. The Discussion is complete and carefully addresses the novelty and the biochemical and biological implications of the findings.

That eggs emit a volatile compound that has antifungal activity is demonstrated by 1) showing that host bees not in direct or indirect contact with P. triangulum eggs get more infected with mold fungi, 2) showing that eggs release an antifungal volatile when placed above a culture of different fungal strains growing on agar plates. That eggs emit NO is demonstrated by histochemical and colorimetric methods and by using fluorescent probes. However, that egg-released NO is responsible for inhibiting fungal growth is only supported by the correlation between the above observations and by previous reports on the mycotic activity of NO. I see the difficulty to genetically prove the causality of NO production in the antifungal effect of egg-derived volatile production. A simple additional experiment may however help to strengthen this hypothesis. It would be important to inhibit NO release in eggs by using L-NAME, the NOS-inhibiting substance used for Figure 6, and to show that egg-induced inhibition of fungal growth on agar plate (as in Figure 3) is abolished or greatly diminished.

Thank you for submitting your article "Nitric oxide radicals are emitted by wasp eggs to kill mold fungi" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by a Reviewing Editor and Ian Baldwin as the Senior Editor.

In response to the reviews you have carried out an additional experiment and have modified the manuscript in various places. As a result the manuscript has been clearly improved. Yet, a few issues still remain.

The additional experiment tests the effect of synthetic NO on fungal infection of honeybees and shows that synthetic NO protects the bees from infection. This experiment was done for logistic reasons as an alternative to the suggested experiment (eliminating NO· from the natural mixture with the inhibitor). The result underlines the involvement of NO but leaves the option of other compounds being involved open. One of the reviewers had commented that the focus on NO is quite directed, and so might result in missing other potential volatile compounds that are also involved in the observed bioactivities. In response to the question to better justify the focus on NO you comment that is not reasonable. If the suggested experiment had been done that might be the case but because the involvement of other compounds has not been excluded I consider it reasonable to explain why you focussed on NO.

In response to the comment that "the observation that larvae are not resistant to NO produced by the eggs is concerning." you respond with comments in the response letter but this has not resulted in a change in the manuscript. It will be important to provide information in the manuscript itself why the larvae will not suffer from NO as this is vital to the understanding of the protective activity of the NO in conserving a resource. This aspect was also identified by one of the other reviewers.

results.result: Beewolf eggs emit a volatile compound that significantly delays fungal growth on honeybee provisions. This effect is observed both when eggs are in direct contact with bees and when bees are exposed to egg volatiles without physical contact, and the effect is mediated by the egg rather than the larva.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 and C8 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental designs (direct contact, volatile exposure, and multiple fungal species) with appropriate statistical analyses (Kaplan-Meier survival analysis with significant p-values). The temporal specificity (effect present before larval hatching, C3) and broad-spectrum activity (C7, C8) strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: The volatile compound from beewolf eggs exhibits broad-spectrum fungicidal activity, completely inhibiting growth of multiple fungal species including Aspergillus flavus, Mucor circinelloides, Penicillium roqueforti, Candida albicans, and Trichophyton rubrum.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7 demonstrate complete inhibition across diverse fungal species with appropriate statistical testing (binomial tests, p<0.001 to p<0.01). The persistence of inhibition after larval removal (C6) provides additional evidence that the effect is due to the egg-produced volatile rather than larval activity.

results.result: Based on odor characteristics, chemical tests, and biological plausibility, the authors hypothesize that the antifungal volatile is nitric oxide (NO·) that oxidizes to nitrogen dioxide (NO2·). This hypothesis is supported by the presence of oxidants in egg headspace and known antimycotic activity of nitrogen oxides.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C15 provide a logical chain of reasoning combining subjective observations (C9), chemical detection (C10), elimination of alternatives (C11-C12), and biological plausibility based on known insect biochemistry (C13-C15). While some evidence is indirect (subjective odor assessment), the iodide/starch test provides objective chemical evidence for oxidants.

results.result: Multiple independent assays confirm that beewolf eggs produce and release NO·. The Griess assay detects NO·/NO2· in egg headspace, and the NO·-specific fluorescent probe DAR4M-AM shows strong fluorescence in beewolf eggs that peaks around one day after oviposition, with minimal fluorescence in control eggs or other Hymenoptera species.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C24 provide strong converging evidence using two independent detection methods (Griess assay and fluorescence microscopy) with appropriate controls (C18, C23) and comparative data from other species (C20-C22). The temporal pattern of fluorescence (C19) aligns with the observed timing of odor emission (C1). Sample sizes are adequate (N=45 for beewolf eggs, N=9-12 for other species).

results.result: Beewolf eggs emit an average of 0.25 ± 0.09 µmol NO· with production peaking 14-15 hours after oviposition at 28°C, with 90% of emission occurring within a two-hour period. The timing is strongly temperature-dependent (Q10 = 2.74), and nitrogen oxides would accumulate to approximately 1690 ± 680 ppm in sealed brood cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C29 provide quantitative measurements using iodometry with adequate sample sizes (N=233 for total emission, N=4 for time course, N=33 for temperature dependence). The calculated Q10 value and estimated brood cell concentrations are based on measured parameters (egg volume N=16, brood cell volume N=250). The sharp temporal peak and temperature dependence are well-characterized.

results.result: Synthetic NO· at 1500 ppm produces antifungal effects comparable to those of beewolf eggs, significantly delaying fungus growth on honeybees. This supports the conclusion that the antifungal effect is predominantly or exclusively due to NO· and its oxidation product NO2·.
results.evaluation: Claims C30 and C51 demonstrate that synthetic NO· at physiologically relevant concentrations produces similar effects to egg-produced gas, with appropriate statistical analysis (Breslow test, p<0.0001). The authors appropriately acknowledge that small amounts of other volatiles cannot be excluded but conclude the effect is predominantly due to nitrogen oxides based on comparable effect sizes (hazard ratios with overlapping confidence intervals).

results.result: The combination of prey embalming and brood cell fumigation with NO·/NO2· provides synergistic antifungal protection beyond either mechanism alone. Embalmed bees with eggs show the least fungal growth, followed by unembalmed bees with eggs, then embalmed bees without eggs, and finally unembalmed bees without eggs.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 provide comprehensive statistical analysis (Kaplan-Meier with pairwise comparisons, all p≤0.003) demonstrating significant differences among all treatment groups for both hyphal growth and conidia formation. Claims C52-C53 offer a plausible mechanistic explanation for synergy based on the chemistry of nitrogen oxides in water, though this remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: A nitric oxide synthase (NOS) located in embryonic tissue is involved in NO· production by beewolf eggs. This is supported by NADPH-diaphorase staining showing NOS activity in embryonic tissue, qRT-PCR showing peak NOS expression at 19-20 hours after oviposition (corresponding to peak NO· emission), and significant reduction in NO· production when eggs are injected with the NOS inhibitor L-NAME but not the non-inhibiting enantiomer D-NAME.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C39 and C64-C67 provide three independent lines of evidence (histochemical, gene expression, and pharmacological inhibition) that converge on NOS involvement. The authors appropriately acknowledge potential alternative explanations (e.g., L-NAME specificity, C67) but conclude the combined evidence strongly supports NOS involvement. The temporal correlation between NOS expression and NO· emission strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: The beewolf genome contains a single NOS gene (9.36 kbp, 25 exons) with high similarity to NOS genes of closely related bees and structural homology to other insects. This is consistent with most invertebrates having only one NOS gene.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 and C68 are supported by gene sequencing data and phylogenetic analysis. The finding of a single NOS gene is consistent with the literature on invertebrate NOS (C40). The structural similarity to other insects (C68) and phylogenetic clustering with bees (C42) provide appropriate comparative context.

results.result: The NOS mRNA in beewolf eggs lacks exon 14 (144 bp) located between the calmodulin and FMN binding domains, in contrast to adult beewolves. This alternative splicing may enable high NO· production, potentially representing convergent evolution with vertebrate inducible NOS (iNOS), which also lacks a regulatory section near the FMN domain.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44 provide direct mRNA sequencing evidence for the missing exon. Claims C69-C70 establish that alternative splicing of NOS is known in other insects. Claims C71-C76 offer a plausible mechanistic explanation based on the known regulatory role of the missing region in vertebrate NOS (C73-C74), though the functional significance remains somewhat speculative (C72, C75-C76). The structural comparison to vertebrate iNOS is intriguing but requires functional validation.

results.result: In beewolf eggs, NOS activity appears to be regulated by gene expression rather than post-translational modification, with expression occurring obligatorily at a specific developmental stage rather than being induced by immunostimulants. The NOS and its alternative splice variant likely play a significant role in brood cell fumigation.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79 draw reasonable inferences from the temporal expression pattern (C37) and structural analysis (C43-C44). The comparison to other systems (Plasmodium-infected mosquitoes, vertebrate iNOS) is appropriate. The authors appropriately acknowledge they cannot exclude additional NO· production pathways (C79), maintaining appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: The estimated NO· concentration in beewolf brood cells (~1500 ppm or 60 µmol/l) and the rate of NO· production (20,000 µmol/kg·h) are extraordinarily high, exceeding concentrations in animal tissues by orders of magnitude and surpassing levels used in medical applications.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 and C63 provide quantitative comparisons with appropriate citations to literature values. The calculations are based on measured NO· emission (C25) and brood cell volume (C28). The authors appropriately note that some loss is expected (C49), making these estimates conservative. The comparisons to medical applications and safety limits provide important context for the magnitude of NO· production.

results.result: Beewolves employ a coordinated, multi-layered antimicrobial defense strategy consisting of: (1) symbiotic bacteria producing antibiotics on cocoons during overwintering, (2) prey embalming with lipids by the mother wasp, and (3) gaseous NO· fumigation by eggs that kills fungi in the immediate environment. This integrated system provides effective protection throughout development.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 and C106 synthesize findings from the current study with prior work (C46-C47 with appropriate citations). The characterization of NO· fumigation as killing rather than merely delaying fungal growth (C48) is supported by the complete inhibition observed in bioassays (C5-C7). The temporal coordination of these defenses across developmental stages is well-established.

results.result: Despite the combined antimicrobial defenses, 5% of beewolf progeny still succumb to fungal infestation in the field. Evolution of fungal resistance to NO·/NO2· is unlikely due to weak selection pressure (beewolf brood cells are rare habitats), lack of repeated exposure, and the high concentrations affecting multiple basic biochemical processes.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 provides field data (with citation) establishing that protection is not perfect. Claims C81-C84 offer logical evolutionary arguments for why resistance is unlikely, supported by citations to known fungal detoxification mechanisms (C84). The reasoning about selection pressure and repeated exposure is sound, though necessarily speculative about future evolutionary trajectories.

results.result: The symbiotic Streptomyces bacteria must survive NO·/NO2· fumigation since they are vertically transmitted and essential for larval survival. Potential survival mechanisms include evolved resistance due to specialization and repeated exposure, spatial separation (bacteria on ceiling, heavier nitrogen oxides accumulate below), physical shielding by hydrocarbon secretions, and possible detoxification by antioxidants.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C90 identify an important biological puzzle (how symbionts survive fumigation) and propose multiple plausible mechanisms, each supported by citations to relevant literature or physical principles. However, all proposed mechanisms are speculative (C87-C90 are all labeled as speculation in evidence_type). No direct experimental evidence is provided to test which, if any, of these mechanisms actually operate. This represents an important area for future research but remains unresolved.

results.result: Brood cell fumigation with NO· likely evolved from small amounts of NO· originally produced for developmental signaling that accidentally provided slight antifungal benefits, leading to strong selection for elevated NO· emission. This represents a key evolutionary innovation and can be viewed as an externalized immune defense.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C96 present a plausible evolutionary scenario supported by citations to relevant concepts (NO· in development, externalized immunity). However, this is entirely speculative reconstruction of evolutionary history without phylogenetic comparative data, ancestral state reconstruction, or experimental evolution. The characterization as a "key evolutionary innovation" (C94) and "externalized immune defense" (C95) are reasonable interpretations but lack direct supporting evidence beyond the functional data.

results.result: Brood cell fumigation likely incurs substantial costs in terms of energy and biochemical resources. NO· synthesis requires L-arginine (an essential amino acid for most insects) and multiple cofactors (FAD, FMN, BH4, NADPH), necessitating that beewolves either evolved the capacity to synthesize L-arginine or that females provision eggs with sufficient L-arginine for both fumigation and embryogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C100 identify legitimate metabolic costs based on well-established biochemistry (C98, C100 with appropriate citations). The inference about L-arginine provisioning or synthesis (C99) is logical given the essential nature of this amino acid in insects. However, no direct measurements of resource allocation or metabolic costs are provided, making the magnitude of costs uncertain even if their existence is well-supported.

results.result: Beewolf embryos survive extraordinarily high concentrations of toxic nitrogen oxides during synthesis, emission, and after release, despite beewolf larvae dying when accidentally exposed. This likely requires concomitant adaptations to protect against NO·/NO2· cytotoxicity, such as carrier molecules to transfer NO· to the egg shell. Understanding these tolerance mechanisms could inspire novel medical applications.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C102 identify a remarkable biological phenomenon (embryo survival vs. larval death) that is well-supported by observations. Claim C103 makes a reasonable inference that protective adaptations must exist. However, claims C104-C105 are entirely speculative about mechanisms, with only an analogy to nitrophorins in blood-sucking insects. No experimental investigation of tolerance mechanisms is provided. The potential for medical applications (C105) is speculative, though the biological question is clearly important.

results.result: Gaseous defenses may be more widespread among underground-developing digger wasps and bees than currently appreciated, given the difficulties of detecting volatiles in subterranean nests. Beewolves offer unique opportunities to study NOS evolution and regulation, as well as NO· production and resistance mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 make reasonable inferences about the potential prevalence of similar defenses based on ecological considerations and detection challenges. The statement about research opportunities (C108) is well-supported by the findings of the study. These are appropriate concluding statements that acknowledge limitations and suggest future directions.

results.result: Background information on beewolf biology and previously known antimicrobial defenses: Beewolf offspring develop in subterranean brood cells on paralyzed honeybees that would be completely overgrown by fungi within three days without countermeasures. Previously documented defenses include prey embalming with hydrocarbons (delaying fungal growth 2-3 days) and symbiotic bacteria producing antibiotics on cocoons during overwintering. Despite embalming, 50% of removed bees show fungal infestation within six days, yet only 5% of progeny succumb to fungi in natural brood cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C120 provide essential background information, all supported by appropriate citations to prior work (primarily Strohm and Linsenmair, Herzner et al., and Kaltenpoth et al.). These claims establish the biological context and justify the search for additional antimicrobial mechanisms. The discrepancy between fungal infestation rates on removed bees (50%, C116) versus mortality in natural brood cells (5%, C117) provides strong motivation for the current study.
